nodes.chainStep: Pediatric assessment triangle (appearance, work of breathing, circulation to the skin), then ABCDE; pulse oximetry and oxygen when the saturation is low (targets differ by condition); a weight, or a Broselow tape estimate
nodes.why: A hands-off look at appearance, work of breathing and circulation to the skin sorts respiratory distress from respiratory failure, and a hands-on ABCDE survey follows. A child in distress is kept in a comfortable position with calm reassurance. Oxygen saturation is measured in every child with suspected bronchiolitis or acute wheeze, and blood gases are not routine. Weight drives every dose; a Broselow tape helps with sizing when the age is unknown.

nodes.summary: Breathless and in shock without an allergen: resuscitate as shock. In children under 10, hypotension is a systolic pressure under 70 plus twice the age in years. A febrile or septic child goes to the shock route of the febrile infant and child pathway (pw_peds_fever): oxygen, IV or IO access, crystalloid boluses reassessed after each, and antibiotics within 1 hour; pneumonia is then treated on its admitted route here. Heart failure and congenital heart disease are not covered in this version.

Cardiac arrest: start CPR with ventilations now, 15:2 for trained healthcare rescuers (30:2 for a single rescuer), because arrests in children often stem from respiratory failure. Paediatric life support is not covered further in this version.

nodes.chainStep: Open the airway, high-concentration oxygen, bag-mask ventilation to visible chest rise at 30 breaths/min for an infant, 20 for a child, 12 for an adolescent; compressions with ventilations for bradycardia with poor perfusion
nodes.why: Respiratory failure needs immediate moves: open the airway, give high-concentration oxygen and start bag-mask ventilation when breathing effort is inadequate, moving to an advanced airway when these fail. Bag-mask ventilation is a reasonable first airway; advanced airways have not beaten it. With a pulse over 60, rescue breaths go at 30 a minute for an infant, 20 for a child and 12 for an adolescent, each only to visible chest rise, avoiding hyperventilation. Hypoxia can cause bradycardia, especially in infants, and compressions with ventilations are for bradycardia with haemodynamic compromise.

nodes.ask: Bronchiolitis picture in an infant. Tests?
options: None routinely; it is a clinical diagnosis, plus oximetry
A chest x-ray to rule out pneumonia before deciding on care
Nasal swab for RSV to confirm it before treating
Blood count and CRP to decide on antibiotics
nodes.chainStep: Clinical diagnosis with pulse oximetry; no routine chest x-ray, blood tests, blood gas or viral testing
nodes.why: Bronchiolitis is diagnosed on a coryzal prodrome of 1 to 3 days followed by persistent cough, fast breathing or recession, and wheeze or crackles, in a child under 2. Oxygen saturation is measured in every case. A chest x-ray is not routine, because changes can mimic pneumonia and should not decide antibiotics, and blood tests and blood gases are not routine either. AAP 2014 diagnoses bronchiolitis on the history and examination, says radiographic and laboratory studies should not be obtained routinely, does not recommend routine virologic testing, and keeps an initial x-ray for respiratory effort severe enough for ICU or signs of an airway complication such as pneumothorax. PREDICT 2025 also advises against viral testing done only for cohorting.

nodes.chainStep: Supportive care: superficial nasal suction for distress or feeding trouble from secretions, oxygen below the saturation threshold, fluids if intake is poor; no bronchodilators, epinephrine, steroids, hypertonic saline, antibiotics or chest physiotherapy
nodes.why: No specific treatment changes the course of bronchiolitis, so care is supportive: superficial suction when secretions cause distress or feeding trouble, oxygen when saturation is persistently low, and fluids when intake falls. NICE says do not use antibiotics, hypertonic saline, nebulized adrenaline, salbutamol, montelukast, ipratropium or corticosteroids; PREDICT 2025 and the 2022 Italian guideline agree. AAP 2014 says no albuterol, no epinephrine, no systemic corticosteroids in any setting, no chest physiotherapy, and no antibiotics without a concomitant bacterial infection or a strong suspicion of one; it no longer recommends the albuterol trial its 2006 version allowed. Hypertonic saline is not given in the emergency department.

nodes.why: Drowsiness or confusion, an absent wheeze, paradoxical breathing and bradycardia mark respiratory arrest as imminent. That means intubation and mechanical ventilation with 100% oxygen, nebulized SABA and ipratropium, IV corticosteroids and intensive care, with a clinician skilled in airway management involved early. results.findings: Known asthma; loud wheeze throughout, no crackles.
